title: Robot OEMs Including KUKA and FANUC Release Hardware Models to Nvidia's SimReady Hub
summary:
Several global automation firms have uploaded simulation-ready versions of their hardware to a free library to facilitate the training of artificial intelligence in virtual settings. The manufacturers, which include KUKA, FANUC, Universal Robots, and Comau, published their equipment models to the NVIDIA SimReady library on Hugging Face, allowing developers to use natural-language search to find and assemble virtual workcells. The move marks a departure from the industry standard of keeping CAD files proprietary and requiring users to use the manufacturers' own closed simulation software.

These contributions are part of a 472GB collection of 2,575 3D assets in the OpenUSD exchange format, covering tools and industrial equipment. The models include physics data, such as measured mass and joint limits, to help researchers build digital twins and train robot policies. The release comes approximately one month after Nvidia announced its acquisition of the Hugging Face hub.

selectedTweets.text:
It’s been just over a month since NVIDIA announced it’s acquiring Hugging Face! 🤯

Anyone can see these two are a perfect match, and they’re clearly already working on something.

@NVIDIARobotics put 2,000+ simulation-ready 3D assets on @huggingface, free and ungated.

Comau. FANUC. Franka Robotics. Robotiq. Standard Bots. Universal Robots. KUKA. 7 OEMs publishing simulation-ready models of their own hardware, in the open, on someone else’s platform.

OEMs have historically kept CAD close and shipped simulation inside their own software: RobotStudio, RoboGuide, KUKA.Sim. 

Publishing a SimReady asset concedes that the scene gets assembled elsewhere, in someone else’s simulator, increasingly by someone else’s agent. 

If your arm isn’t in the library, whatever assembles the workcell picks one that is.

On the substance: a CAD model is not a simulation asset. Simulation needs collision geometry, mass and inertia, friction, joint structure and limits, semantic labels, sensor attributes.

The part I’d watch is profiles. SimReady Foundation defines what an asset must carry for a given use case, with validation tools to check it. 

That’s what makes a mixed-supplier library composable instead of a pile of models with inconsistent units, origins and collision conventions.

And it’s indexed for agents. Natural-language search across the library, so a model can find assets, reference them into a USD stage and write the code that assembles the cell.

Third time this month I’ve written about that same shape. The agent produces a scene or a config, a human reviews the file.

2,000 assets is a good start!

🔗 Start building yourself: https://t.co/rWMV6d1OMQ
